chapters.context: Getting started with R Learning outcomes After this chapter, you should be able to distinguish R from RStudio and Quarto, create a project, run and save commands, and install and load a package. This overview updates the original lecture discussion with a focused selection of current tools and a dedicated RAISINS lesson. The original notes remain archived; the course calculations use R. Data science is a fast growing field with the development of advanced statistical tools for data analysis and visualization. When the data volume is large and also when precision is required, we depend on statistical software to get better insights from the data. Statistical software makes analysis easy, produces more precise results, enables us to use complex statistical tools and generates advance complex graphical outputs. One cannot blindly depend upon statistical software for data analysis, as you can use any software for data analysis as per your convenience. Even some of the basic statistical tools, you can perform calculations manually. Without proper knowledge in statistics, every software is a garbage in garbage out. What that really matters is knowledge in statistical concepts and tools, so that effective interpretations can be made from the data. Agricultural experiments demand a wide range of statistical tools for analysis, which includes exploratory analysis, design of experiments, and statistical genetics. It is a challenge for scientists and students to find a suitable platform for data analysis and publish the research outputs in quality journals. Statistical software differs in cost, licensing, interface, and analytical capabilities. The open source programming language R and associated ecosystem of packages, provides an excellent platform for data analysis and is widely used in agricultural teaching and research. Insufficient programming and computational knowledge are the primary challenges for agricultural researchers using R for analysis. In our sessions, I will be using R studio. Agricultural scientists and students need not become professional software developers, but they should learn enough programming to understand, adapt, and reproduce their analyses. I have seen agricultural researchers take up R workshops and leave it behind as such workshops mainly deals with code chunks; user will get easily tired of that. Beauty of R is that, it is a free open-source software. Apart from the software used, I again insist that students and researchers should strengthen their basic statistics knowledge and they should be able to decide, what tool should be used and when. I strongly recommend that you should go through the basic statistical theory by visiting my e-book Textbook of Agricultural Statistics. Before proceeding further, one should also have a basic knowledge about different statistical software available. Statistical software for agricultural analysis Statistical software helps us organize observations, fit models, visualize relationships, and communicate results. Agricultural applications include summarizing soil properties, comparing treatments in field experiments, modelling growth, and examining associations between weather and yield. The choice of software should follow the scientific question, experimental design, and need to reproduce the analysis. Understanding access, licences, and interfaces Open-source software provides source code under a licence that specifies how it may be used, modified, and redistributed. Free of charge describes cost; it does not, by itself, establish that source code is available. Public-domain software has a different legal status from software distributed under an open-source licence. Commercial software and hosted services may require a licence or subscription, although trials, educational access, or limited preview modes may be available. An interface is another consideration. A command-based environment records an analysis as instructions that can be inspected and rerun. A graphical interface lets the analyst choose variables and options through menus. A web application runs through a browser. These categories can overlap a graphical web application may use R for its calculations, while R itself can be used through an editor such as RStudio. Check the current provider documentation for access conditions and supported analyses. A focused comparison of current tools The following selection was reviewed on 16 October 2026. It emphasizes tools relevant to this course rather than attempting a catalogue of every statistical program. | Tool | Main role | Relevance to an undergraduate agricultural practical | |---|---|---| | R | Open-source language and environment for statistics and graphics | The computational foundation of this book; students save commands, inspect models, and reproduce results. | | RStudio | An integrated development environment with an open-source Desktop edition | Provides the script editor, Console, object browser, plots, and project tools used in the practicals. Install R as well. | | Quarto | An open-source scientific publishing system | Combines explanations, executable R code, tables, and figures into reports and books. | | RAISINS | A browser-based agricultural analysis platform | Offers guided modules for statistical analysis and experimental designs; useful for demonstrations and comparison with an R analysis. Access depends on the module and available plan. | | jamovi | A free, open statistical spreadsheet powered by R | Provides an approachable graphical route into statistical analysis and a useful bridge to R. | | JASP | Free, open-source statistical software with a graphical interface | Supports classical and Bayesian analyses, helping students compare statistical approaches and read structured output. | | Genstat | Commercial statistical software with agricultural applications | Provides another environment for experimental-design analysis and related research methods where an institutional licence is available. | Official sources R Project, RStudio documentation, Quarto, RAISINS, jamovi, JASP, and Genstat. The earlier long list of general and specialist programs has been replaced with this teaching-focused selection. Software absent from the table is not necessarily discontinued or unsuitable for another discipline. For this course, students need R, RStudio, and Quarto; other interfaces provide complementary learning opportunities. RAISINS RAISINS (R and AI Solutions in INferential Statistics) is a browser-based platform for agricultural data analysis developed by Statoberry LLP with mentorship from agricultural statisticians at Kerala Agricultural University. It combines R, Python, and AI assistance in a graphical interface, without requiring a local installation. Its modules include descriptive statistics, t-tests, correlation, regression, experimental designs, nonparametric methods, and statistical genetics. Students can explore completely randomized, randomized block, factorial, and split-plot analyses through guided modules. RAISINS website. To begin, choose a module, inspect its sample dataset or data template, select the required variables, and run the analysis. Preview mode uses built-in datasets; analysing your own data requires suitable access. RAISINS complements the R programming taught in this book students should understand the experimental design, check model assumptions, and interpret the output themselves, including any AI-generated explanation. See the getting-started guide. Why this textbook uses R For agricultural researchers I recommend learning R through RStudio students can develop scripts, inspect objects, produce graphics, and keep a record of their decisions. A package supplies additional functions; an interface helps us use them. Our agricultural package grapesAgri1 is an additional resource, while the core lessons show the underlying R calculations. RAISINS offers a complementary guided route, and Quarto brings code and explanation together in the final report. R R is a programming language for statistical computing and graphics supported by the R Core Team and the R Foundation for Statistical Computing. Created by statisticians Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman. R is an implementation of the S programming language. R is used among data miners, bioinformaticians and statisticians for data analysis and developing statistical software. Users have created packages to augment the functions of the R language. According to user surveys and studies of scholarly literature databases, R is one of the most commonly used programming languages used in data mining. The official R software environment is an open-source free software environment within the GNU package, available under the GNU General Public License. It is written primarily in C, Fortran, and R itself (partially self-hosting). R has a command line interface. Multiple third-party graphical user interfaces are also available, such as RStudio, an integrated development environment. Rstudio RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R. It includes a console, syntax-highlighting editor that supports direct code execution, as well as tools for plotting, history, debugging and workspace management. RStudio is available in open source and commercial editions and runs on the desktop (Windows, Mac, and Linux) or in a browser connected to RStudio Server. RStudio is a free and open-source integrated development environment (IDE) for R, a programming language for statistical computing and graphics. JJ Allaire, creator of the programming language ColdFusion, founded RStudio. RStudio is available in two editions RStudio Desktop, where the program is run locally as a regular desktop application; and RStudio Server, which allows accessing RStudio using a web browser while it is running on a remote Linux server. The original RStudio interface used the Qt framework; the current desktop application uses Electron. RStudio combines components written in several programming languages. Work on RStudio started at around December 2010, and the first public beta version (v0.92) was officially announced in February 2011. Typical RStudio window has four panes as explained below 1. Console This is where the action happens. Here any authentic R code typed after the ‘>’ prompt will be executed after pressing ‘Enter’ to generate the output. We will use the Console to run and inspect the commands developed in this book. 2. Source Editor This is where R scripts (collection of code) can be created and edited. New R script can be opened by clicking File --> New File --> R Script or using short cut ctrl+shift+N. You can type your codes here. To run a code in console or execute, place the cursor in the line which code is written and press ctrl+enter or highlight the code you wish to evaluate and clicking on the “Run” button on the top right of the Source. You can save your R codes, written in script. 3. Environment|History|Connections All of the data objects (such as vectors, matrices, and dataframes) that you have defined in your current R session are listed under the Environment tab of this panel. In data objects, you may also examine details like the quantity of observations and rows. A few other clickable options are available on the tab, such as Import Dataset, which will launch a graphical user interface (GUI) for inputting data into R. This panel's History tab only provides a history of all the code that you have previously evaluated in the Console. The Environment / History panel could be helpful as you become more accustomed to R. However, you can ignore it right now. You can simply just reduce the window by clicking the minimise button in the panel's upper right corner if you wish to clear up space on your screen. 4. Files|Plots|Packages|Help|Viewer You can find a collection of useful information in the Files|Plots|Packages|Help panel. Let's examine each tab in more detail - The file directory on your hard disc is accessible through the files panel. You can utilise the "Files" panel to set your working directory by clicking "More" and then "Set As Working Directory" once you've navigated to the folder where you wish to read and save files. - All of your plots are displayed in the Plots panel. There are buttons to export the plot as a pdf or jpg and to open the plot in a separate window. We are interested in the install button in this pane, to install packages required for our analysis. Repositories A repository is where packages are located so that they can be installed from it. Organizations and developers each have their own local repository, which is often online and open to all. The most well-liked R package repositories include CRAN, BIOCONDUCTOR, GITHUB. CRAN Comprehensive R Archive Network(CRAN) is the official repository, It is an international network of ftp and web servers run and managed by the R community. It is coordinated by the R community, and before a package can be published in CRAN, it must pass a number of tests to guarantee that it complies with CRAN rules. Bioconductor Open source software for bioinformatics is designed for the topic-specific repository known as Bioconductor. In keeping with CRAN, it has its own submission and review procedures, and its community is quite active, holding numerous conferences and meetings each year. Github The most well-known repository for open source projects is Github. Its popularity is due to the unrestricted open source storage space, integration with the version control programme git, and simplicity of sharing and teamwork. Base packages Base packages or standard pacakges come pre-installed with R installations and are regarded as being a part of the R source code. The fundamental R functions are found in base packages, which make it possible to perform common statistical and graphical operations on datasets. Examples of Base packages include stats, graphics, grDevices, utils, datasets, methods and base. The functions available in these Base packages can be used for basic operations on the data set. Some of the functions we have discussed earlier in Section @sec-language, like mean(),min, log10,as.data.frame etc. The standard installation contains base packages for essential language, statistical, graphics, and utility functions. The exact installed list can be inspected with installed.packages(). In addition, there are fifteen "recommended packages" from CRAN which are included with binary distributions of R KernSmooth, MASS, Matrix, boot, class, cluster, codetools, foreign, lattice, mgcv, nlme, nnet, rpart, spatial, and survival. A first agricultural calculation Suppose a 20-square-metre harvested plot produces 9.6 kg of grain. One hectare contains 10,000 square metres, and one tonne contains 1,000 kg. The answer is 4.8 t/ha. The expression makes the unit conversion explicit. It does not adjust for grain moisture, harvested border rows, or sampling errors; those require additional information. Names such as grain_kg help prevent unit mistakes. <- assigns a value. A line beginning with is a comment. R is case sensitive grain_kg and Grain_kg are different names. The Console's > prompt is not part of the code. A + prompt usually means that a bracket or quotation mark has not been closed; press Escape and inspect the command. Packages and help A package supplies functions, documentation, and sometimes datasets. Install a package once into an R library, then load it in each new session where it is needed. Installation should be a deliberate setup step, not part of rendering an analysis. The notation dplyrfilter() calls a function explicitly from a package. It is useful when packages provide functions with the same name. For Bioconductor packages, use the current Bioconductor installation instructions and BiocManager; the old biocLite() approach in the earlier notes is obsolete. Errors are information “Object not found” suggests a misspelt name, an unrun assignment, or an object from a previous session. “Could not find function” suggests a misspelling or an unloaded package. “Cannot open file” suggests an incorrect relative path. Start with the first error and run a small piece of code that reproduces it. Restart R periodically and run your saved script from the beginning; this reveals hidden dependencies on old objects. sections.body: Values and vectors An atomic vector holds values of one underlying type. Combining numbers and text causes coercion, usually to character. Numeric values support arithmetic; character values describe names; logical values represent TRUE or FALSE. A factor records categories with a specified set of levels. R indexes from 1. Square brackets select elements. > compares values; == tests equality; != tests inequality; and %in% tests membership. Use & and | for elementwise “and” and “or”. Arithmetic is vectorized. sections.title: Why a cleaning log matters
sections.body: A field sheet may contain a repeated entry, a missed harvest, or a measurement in the wrong unit. These are different problems. A duplicate entry may be removed after checking its identity; a missing harvest remains unknown; and a unit error requires evidence before correction. A cleaning log records the identifier, issue, action, reason, and source of verification. The supplied crop_dirty.csv is a teaching copy with deliberate problems. sections.title: A grammar of data manipulation
sections.body: select() chooses columns, filter() chooses rows, mutate() creates or changes columns, arrange() orders rows, and summarise() reduces observations to summaries. group_by() controls the groups within which later operations occur. These verbs express a sequence of data operations; the pipe passes each result to the next step. filter() keeps rows where its condition is TRUE; an NA condition is not retained. State explicitly whether missing records should be included. mutate() generally preserves the number of rows; summarise() changes the observational level. The treatment table has one row per treatment, whereas the original table has one row per plot. It cannot support analyses that require individual plot variation. .groups = "drop" prevents accidental retention of grouping in later operations. If every yield in a group is missing, mean(..., na.rm = TRUE) returns NaN; handle that group as having no usable estimate.

sections.title: Soil and weather summaries
sections.body: Summing monthly rainfall gives annual rainfall when all 12 months are present. Averaging monthly temperature means gives equal weight to months, not days; use day weights if the question requires a mean over days. A mean of yields is not a production-weighted regional yield unless the areas are equal.

sections.title: Joining tables safely
sections.body: A join links records by keys. Here the soil table has one record per plot. Verify key uniqueness and unmatched records before accepting a join. Many-to-many joins can silently multiply observations and change subsequent averages. left_join() retains all rows of the first table, adding NA when there is no match. inner_join() retains only matched rows. A row count check is necessary but not sufficient inspect identifier meaning and measurement timing too.

sections.title: Wide and long forms
sections.body: Wide tables put several measurements in separate columns; long tables use a variable column and a value column. Long form is convenient for grouped graphics. Do not average nitrogen and phosphorus merely because both are expressed in mg/kg. They are distinct quantities. Reshaping changes representation, not scientific meaning.

sections.title: Understanding what happens inside a grouped operation
sections.body: When we write group_by(treatment), R does not immediately replace the observations with treatment means. It adds grouping information to the table. The next operation then acts within each group. This distinction explains why mutate() and summarise() can give very different tables after the same grouping command. The first result still has 60 plot rows. Every plot carries its treatment's mean and its own deviation from that mean. The summary table has only three treatment rows. If the purpose is to investigate within-treatment variation, the first table is useful. If the purpose is a compact reporting table, the second is useful. Neither representation should be confused with additional independent replication. The word n() counts rows in a group. It does not automatically count nonmissing yields. Thus a group can have ten rows but only eight observed yields. The quantities n(), sum(!is.na(yield_t_ha)), and mean(yield_t_ha, na.rm = TRUE) must be interpreted together.

sections.title: Weighted means and unequal harvested areas
sections.body: Let us suppose two farms harvest 1 ha and 9 ha, with yields of 2 and 6 t/ha respectively. Their arithmetic mean yield is 4 t/ha. However, total production is 56 tonnes on 10 ha, so the area-weighted yield is 5.6 t/ha. Both calculations are arithmetically correct; they answer different questions. The arithmetic mean describes the average yield of these two farm records when each farm receives equal weight. The weighted mean describes production per hectare across their combined harvested area. Before reporting a district, season, or treatment summary, ask what should receive equal weight. A column of weights must have a scientific interpretation; arbitrary weights cannot improve an analysis merely by changing the result.

sections.title: Joining is not matching by row position
sections.body: If soil rows have been sorted by pH while crop rows remain sorted by plot number, using cbind() to combine them would attach soil measurements to the wrong plots. A join uses an identifier instead. We can demonstrate this by deliberately changing the soil row order. The pH values remain correctly aligned because the join uses plot_id. A correct key is therefore more valuable than a visually tidy row order. For data collected at several depths or dates, plot_id alone may not be unique; the key might need plot_id, depth_cm, and sampling_date. A one-to-many relationship can be legitimate, but the resulting observational unit must be stated.

sections.body: A box and whisker plot, often known as a box plot, shows a data set's five-number summary. The minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum make up the five-number summary. A box is drawn from the first quartile to the third quartile in a box plot. chapters.title: An exploratory study of crop yield
chapters.objectives: Organize an exploratory analysis around a question, combine summaries with graphics, distinguish observed association from causation, and formulate a defensible follow-up analysis.

sections.title: Begin with a question and design
sections.body: Our teaching question is Which recorded characteristics are associated with differences in grain yield? The simulated trial has 60 plot records five blocks, three management treatments, and two varieties with two replicate plots per combination. Nitrogen application is closely linked to management treatment. Thus, an association between nitrogen and yield may also reflect other treatment differences. Soil observations are linked by plot identifier. EDA is a structured investigation of distributions, patterns, anomalies, and relationships. It generates and refines questions. Repeatedly searching for a small p-value and reporting only the successful test would give a misleading impression of evidence.

sections.title: Examine distributions before relationships
sections.body: Look for balance, within-group variation, block shifts, and unusual observations. A high-yielding treatment in one block may behave differently elsewhere. A graph of every plot is more informative than treatment means alone.

sections.title: Examine candidate relationships
sections.body: These relationships need scientific interpretation. Does the predictor precede the response? Was it manipulated or only measured? Are measurements at the same spatial scale? In a real trial, assigning the same weather-station value to many plots does not create independent rainfall replicates. The teaching dataset varies plot-level water exposure for illustration; this must not be mistaken for many independent weather stations.

sections.title: Write an EDA memo
sections.body: An effective memo states the question, source and design, cleaning decisions, two or three supported patterns, and their limitations. For example “Treatment-specific plots suggest differences in yield, with additional variation among blocks. Nitrogen and treatment are linked, so their separate effects cannot be inferred from a pooled scatter plot. A model should represent the experimental design before adding exploratory predictors.” Do not invent numerical findings in prose. Extract values from your executed summaries and identify the relevant table or figure. Separate what the data show from what you propose as an explanation.

sections.title: From an agricultural question to a sequence of comparisons
sections.body: A common difficulty in EDA is deciding where to begin. Students often calculate every available summary and draw several graphs, but cannot explain why each was needed. A more useful approach is to translate the question into a small sequence of comparisons. For our yield question, begin with the response is yield measured on the same basis for every plot? chapters.title: Modelling crop growth
chapters.objectives: Interpret logistic and Gompertz growth parameters, fit nonlinear models, assess residuals and parameter plausibility, and recognize the limits of extrapolation and repeated measurements.

sections.title: Why straight lines are often inadequate
sections.body: During establishment a crop may accumulate little biomass; rapid growth follows, then growth slows as resources become limiting or maturity approaches. A straight line cannot represent all three phases. A sigmoid model describes an S-shaped trajectory using parameters that have biological interpretations. Let W(t) denote biomass at time t. One parameterization of the logistic curve is W(t)=\frac}, \qquad A>0,\ k>0. A is the asymptotic biomass, k controls the rate of approach, and t_i is the time of inflection. At t_i, biomass is A/2 and absolute growth rate is maximal at Ak/4. The Gompertz form used here is W(t)=A\exp\. Its inflection occurs at biomass A/e, and its maximum absolute growth rate is Ak/e. Both have an upper asymptote, but the logistic is symmetric around its inflection whereas the Gompertz is asymmetric. Parameter meanings depend on the chosen formula; a package using other symbols may use a different parameterization.

sections.title: Understand the growth dataset
sections.body: growth.csv contains simulated biomass in g/m² at 12 sampling times, with three independently harvested quadrats at each time. The independence assumption is part of this teaching design. Repeated measurements on the same plants require a model accounting for within-plant dependence, beyond ordinary independent-error nls(). Before fitting, ask whether the observations span early growth, the inflection region, and a plateau. Without late observations the asymptote can be poorly identified even when the fitted curve looks convincing.

sections.title: Fit and compare curves
sections.body: Nonlinear least squares chooses parameters that minimize the sum of squared residuals. Starting values guide its numerical search; they are not prior evidence. Here a plateau near 1,000 g/m², an inflection near day 50, and a positive growth rate are reasonable visual starting points. Compare AIC only for fits to the same response observations under comparable error assumptions. Lower AIC suggests a better balance of fit and complexity among the candidates; it does not prove biological truth. Do not compare raw-response and log-response AIC values without accounting for the transformed likelihood.

sections.title: Diagnostics and interpretation
sections.body: A curved residual pattern suggests a missing feature of the growth curve. Increasing residual spread suggests changing error variance. Check convergence, sensible parameter values, and sensitivity to starting values. Nonconvergence may reflect poor starting values, inadequate data coverage, or an unsuitable model; increasing iteration limits alone is not a scientific solution. The curve predicts a mean trajectory, not a guaranteed individual observation. predict.nls() does not automatically provide valid confidence or prediction intervals from an interval argument as predict.lm() does. Uncertainty may require an appropriate bootstrap or another justified method. Avoid presenting an unqualified long-term biomass forecast from a short growth experiment.

sections.title: Seeing the role of each parameter
sections.body: It is easy to read a formula and still be unsure how its parameters affect the graph. Let us change one parameter at a time while keeping the others fixed. Begin with a logistic curve having an asymptote of 1,000 g/m², a rate parameter of 0.07 per day, and an inflection time of day 50. Increasing A raises the upper plateau. Increasing k makes the transition from early growth to the plateau more rapid. Increasing ti moves the rapid-growth phase later in time. These changes can compensate for one another over a short observed interval, which explains why parameters may be unstable when observations do not cover the whole trajectory. The logistic scale parameter used by R's SSlogis() is another way of expressing the same curve. In its usual form, scal is 1/k. Thus a larger scal corresponds to a slower transition, whereas a larger k corresponds to a faster transition. Comparing printed parameter names without checking formulas can therefore reverse an interpretation.

chapters.context: Agricultural time series and forecasting Learning outcomes Construct a regular time series, distinguish trend from seasonality, calculate moving averages, fit an introductory ARIMA model, and evaluate forecasts using a chronological holdout and a baseline. The detailed examples from the original time-series chapter are retained English kings, monthly births, souvenir sales, and London rainfall. They teach time-series structure before the agricultural weather application. Local copies are supplied so a classroom render does not depend on a live download. These are historical series, not simulated agricultural observations. The data appendix records the original sources and units. We will be using the following data to demonstrate Time series analysis in R. Download the data and save in your system for practice. -kings.csv contains data on the age of death of successive kings of England, starting with William the Conqueror. -births.csv is a data set of monthly births in New York City, in thousands, from January 1946 to December 1959 (originally collected by Newton). -souvenir.csv contains monthly sales for a souvenir shop at a beach resort town in Queensland, Australia, for January 1987-December 1993. -rain.csv data contains total annual rainfall in inches for London, from 1813-1912. Getting Started After importing the time series data kings.csv into R in the name kings, the next step is to save it as a time series object using R's ts() function. For example, to store the data from your imported CSV file in the variable 'kings' as a time series, you would write Import kings.csv and call it as kings in R. (We assume the reader knows the basics of importing csv in R) If your time series data is collected at intervals shorter than a year, like monthly or quarterly, you can use the frequency parameter in the ts() function. For monthly data, set frequency=12, and for quarterly data, set frequency=4. You can also indicate the starting year and interval with the start parameter. For instance, if the data begins in the second quarter of 1986, you'd use start=c(1986, 2). Use the bundled data/original-births.csv file described in the first section which contains number of births per month in New York city, from January 1946 to December 1959. So it can be converted to ts object in R as follows. It is a monthly data so frequency 12. similarly for souvenir.csv Plotting time series data After importing a time series into R, the next step is often to create a plot of the data. You can do this using the plot.ts() function. For example, to plot the time series of the ages at death of 42 successive English kings, you would write In the time plot, the fluctuations in the data appear to be relatively consistent in size throughout the series. This suggests that an additive model could be appropriate for describing this time series. In an additive model, the components (trend, seasonality, and residuals) are added together, which works well when the variability (the size of fluctuations) does not change much over time. The time series shows a pattern of seasonal variation in monthly births, with peaks in the summer and dips in the winter. This suggests that an additive model could be suitable, as the size of the seasonal fluctuations remains fairly constant and does not seem influenced by the overall level of the series. Additionally, the random variations in the data appear to stay relatively stable over time. In this case, an additive model doesn't seem suitable because both the seasonal and random fluctuations increase as the time series level rises. To make the data more suitable for an additive model, we may need to apply a transformation. One common approach is to take the natural logarithm of the original data, which can help stabilize the variance and make the fluctuations more consistent across the series. In the log-transformed time series, the size of both the seasonal and random fluctuations appears relatively stable over time and does not seem to vary with the overall level of the series. This suggests that the log-transformed data is now more suitable for an additive model, as the fluctuations are more uniform throughout the time series. Decomposing Time Series Decomposing a time series involves breaking it down into distinct elements to better understand its underlying patterns. Typically, this process separates the data into three key components 1. Trend Component This reflects the long-term direction of the data, showing whether there is an overall upward or downward movement over time. It helps to identify the general course of the series without short-term fluctuations. 2. Seasonal Component If the data exhibits regular patterns at consistent intervals, this component captures those repeating cycles. For example, monthly sales data may show higher sales during the holiday season every year. This helps to isolate predictable fluctuations from the rest of the data. 3. Irregular (or Residual) Component After removing the trend and seasonal components, what's left is the irregular component, which represents random noise or short-term variations that cannot be attributed to a clear pattern. These fluctuations are unpredictable and often occur due to unforeseen events or natural variability. By decomposing a time series, you can better analyze and model the individual components, making it easier to forecast future values or understand the underlying behaviors of the data. Decomposing Non-Seasonal Data A non-seasonal time series typically consists of a trend component and an irregular component. Decomposing this type of time series involves estimating these two components separately. To estimate the trend component of a non-seasonal time series that can be modeled using an additive approach, a common technique is to apply a smoothing method. One effective method for this is the simple moving average (SMA), which helps to smooth out short-term fluctuations and highlight longer-term trends. In R, you can use the SMA() function from the "TTR" package to calculate the simple moving average of your time series data. Here is how to do it 1. Install the "TTR" Package If you haven't already installed the "TTR" package, you can do so by running the following command in R 2. Load the "TTR" Package Once the package is installed, you can load it into your R session with the following command After loading the package, you can then use the SMA() function to compute the simple moving average and obtain the trend component of your non-seasonal time series. This process allows you to better understand the underlying trend in the data by reducing noise from irregular fluctuations. Although smoothing the time series with a simple moving average of order 3 has helped reduce some fluctuations, there are still considerable random variations present. To achieve a more accurate estimation of the trend component, it may be beneficial to apply a higher-order moving average. Finding the optimal level of smoothing often requires some trial and error to determine the best order that balances noise reduction while preserving the essential patterns in the data. For instance, you can experiment with a simple moving average of order 8 to see if this provides a clearer representation of the trend. Here’s how you can do that in R Using a higher order like 8 should help smooth the data further, potentially reducing the random fluctuations and allowing for a clearer view of the underlying trend. This iterative approach can lead to a more accurate understanding of the time series behavior. Decomposing Seasonal Data A seasonal time series is characterized by three components a trend component, a seasonal component, and an irregular component. Decomposing this time series involves separating it into these three distinct elements to better understand its structure. To estimate the trend and seasonal components of a seasonal time series that can be modeled using an additive approach, you can utilize the decompose() function in R. This function effectively breaks down the time series into its constituent components, providing estimates for each. Here’s how to use the decompose() function 1. Apply the decompose() Function You can call this function on your seasonal time series object. For example 2. Accessing Components The decompose() function returns a list object containing the estimates of the seasonal, trend, and irregular components. You can access these components using the following names - birthstscompseasonal This element holds the estimated seasonal component. - birthstscomptrend This contains the estimated trend component. - birthstscomprandom This represents the irregular component. By decomposing the time series, you can analyze each component separately, which can enhance your understanding of the data and improve forecasting accuracy. Inspect the twelve seasonal factors returned by the decomposition. Their scale is thousands of births. Positive factors identify months above the estimated trend and negative factors identify months below it; compare tapply(birthstscompseasonal, cycle(birthsts), mean) rather than relying on a remembered month or value. To visualize these components—trend, seasonal, and irregular—you can use the plot() function in R. Here is how to do it 1. Plot the Components After decomposing your time series, you can create plots for each component as follows This command will generate a series of plots showing the estimated trend, seasonal, and irregular components of your time series, allowing you to analyze and interpret the behavior of each component visually. The plot presented above displays the original time series at the top, followed by the estimated trend component, the estimated seasonal component, and finally, the estimated irregular component at the bottom. The trend component reveals a slight decline from approximately 24 in 1947 to around 22 in 1948. After this dip, there is a consistent upward trend, reaching about 27 by 1959. If the time series can be described using an additive model, this process is relatively straightforward. By estimating the seasonal component and subtracting it from the original data, you can remove the seasonal variation and obtain a seasonally adjusted time series. Here’s how to achieve this in R using the decompose() function 1. Estimate the Seasonal Component First, decompose the time series to estimate its seasonal component using the decompose() function. This function calculates the seasonal, trend, and irregular components of the data. 2. Subtract the Seasonal Component Once you have the seasonal component, subtract it from the original time series to remove the seasonality. This gives you a seasonally adjusted series 3. Interpretation The result is a time series without the repetitive seasonal fluctuations, making it easier to focus on trends and irregular components. For example, if you're analyzing the number of births per month in New York City, this adjustment will help you see whether the overall trend in births is increasing or decreasing, without being influenced by regular seasonal peaks and troughs. By seasonally adjusting the data, analysts can make more accurate comparisons and forecasts without seasonal noise. This process is crucial in understanding the true underlying behavior of time series data, especially when making decisions based on long-term trends. We can then plot the seasonally adjusted time series using the plot() function Forecasts Using Exponential Smoothing Exponential smoothing, first introduced by Robert Goodell Brown in 1956 and later refined by Charles C. Holt in 1957, is a widely effective technique for smoothing time-series data. Unlike methods like the simple moving average, which apply equal weights to past data points, exponential smoothing uses an exponentially decreasing weight function. This approach assigns more significance to recent observations and less to older ones. A key parameter in this method is the smoothing constant, which determines the rate of decay for the weights. Due to its straightforward nature and ease of application, exponential smoothing is frequently employed in time-series analysis, often incorporating factors like seasonality based on user-defined assumptions. Exponential smoothing is generally used to make short term forecasts, but longer-term forecasts using this technique can be quite unreliable. When the smoothing factor (α) is larger, the level of smoothing decreases. An α value close to 1 results in less smoothing, giving more weight to recent changes in the data. Conversely, an α value closer to 0 leads to greater smoothing, making the model less responsive to recent fluctuations. There is no single alpha value suitable for every series; estimation and forecast evaluation are needed. In some cases, the statistician’s expertise is used to choose an appropriate factor. Alternatively, statistical methods can be applied to optimize α, such as using the least squares method to find the value that minimizes the sum of errors in the model. Types of Exponential Smoothing 1. Simple Exponential Smoothing - Best suited for data without trend or seasonality. - The forecast for the next period is a weighted average of past observations, where weights decrease exponentially for older observations. - The smoothing parameter (\(\alpha\)) controls the degree of weighting; values range from 0 to 1. A higher \(\alpha\) gives more weight to recent observations. Formula \[ F_ = \alpha Y_t + (1 - \alpha) F_t \] where \(F_\) is the forecast for the next period, \(Y_t\) is the actual observation at time \(t\), and \(F_t\) is the forecast for time \(t\). 2. Holt’s Linear Exponential Smoothing - Extends simple exponential smoothing to account for trends in the data. - It uses two smoothing parameters one for the level (\(\alpha\)) and one for the trend (\(\beta\)). - This method allows for forecasts that can accommodate linear trends. Formulas - Level \[ l_t = \alpha Y_t + (1 - \alpha)(l_ + b_) \] - Trend \[ b_t = \beta (l_t - l_) + (1 - \beta)b_ \] - Forecast \[ F_ = l_t + mb_t \] 3. Holt-Winters Exponential Smoothing - An extension of Holt’s method that also incorporates seasonality. - It uses three parameters \(\alpha\) for the level, \(\beta\) for the trend, and \(\gamma\) for the seasonal component. - There are two variants additive (for seasonal effects that are roughly constant) and multiplicative (for seasonal effects that change with the level of the series). Formulas - Level \[ l_t = \alpha (Y_t / s_) + (1 - \alpha)(l_ + b_) \] - Trend \[ b_t = \beta (l_t - l_) + (1 - \beta)b_ \] - Seasonal \[ s_t = \gamma (Y_t / l_t) + (1 - \gamma)s_ \] - Forecast \[ F_ = (l_t + mb_t)s_ \] Advantages of Exponential Smoothing - Simplicity It is relatively easy to implement and understand. - Flexibility Different types can accommodate various data patterns (trends and seasonality). - Adaptability The method can quickly adjust to changes in the data patterns. Exponential smoothing is a powerful technique for forecasting time series data. By applying weighted averages to past observations, it effectively captures trends and seasonal patterns, making it a valuable tool for analysts and decision-makers. The method's adaptability and ease of use make it an essential part of any forecasting toolkit. Consider the data rain.csv In the above plot we can observe that the mean remains approximately constant at around 25 inches, and the random fluctuations appear to be relatively stable over time. Given this, it seems appropriate to apply an additive model for the time series. Consequently, we can generate forecasts using simple exponential smoothing. Its fitted component contains in-sample fitted values; it is not a vector of future forecasts. The forecast results are saved in a list variable like rainforecast, and the predicted values can be accessed through its fitted element. This SSE value is stored in the SSE element of the rainforecast list. In this case, the sum of squared errors (SSE) is 1828.855. For instance, in London's rainfall data, the initial value is 23.56 inches for the year 1813. To specify this initial level value in the HoltWinters() function, you can use the l.start parameter. Moving averages and decomposition A trailing three-month average uses the current and previous two months. A centred average also uses future observations relative to its centre, so it is suitable for retrospective description but not directly available at a forecast origin. Larger windows smooth more but can hide rapid changes. stl() here assumes a fixed seasonal pattern through s.window = "periodic"; inspect whether that is reasonable. ARIMA as a starting model ARIMA combines autoregression (dependence on past values), differencing (changes between successive values), and moving-average error terms (dependence on past shocks). The notation ARIMA(p,d,q) gives their orders. Seasonal terms have analogous orders and a seasonal period. The moving-average term in ARIMA is not the same as a simple rolling mean of observations. Automatic selection searches candidate models under an information criterion. It cannot determine whether a forecast is useful for an agricultural decision. Fit only on the training period and compare predictions with a simple alternative. The seasonal naive baseline predicts each month using the value from the corresponding month of the previous year. Compare holdout RMSE and MAE, not only in-sample errors. MAPE is problematic near zero, common in rainfall. A model that loses to a baseline has not earned its complexity. For stronger evaluation, use rolling forecast origins and report accuracy by forecast horizon. Check residuals and communicate uncertainty The residual time plot reveals changing spread or isolated shocks; the autocorrelation function identifies remaining temporal patterns; and a Ljung–Box test checks a set of residual autocorrelations. A large p-value does not prove independence. A good forecast should also be plausible an unconstrained Gaussian model may generate negative rainfall predictions. Consider suitable transformations or nonnegative models rather than silently replacing negative forecasts with zero. Prediction intervals describe uncertain future observations under the model. They do not guarantee that all future values lie inside them. Changes in climate, instrumentation, or management can invalidate historical relationships. sections.title: From description to inference
sections.body: Descriptive statistics summarize observed data. Inference uses a sampling or randomization model to reason about an unobserved population or treatment effect. The experimental unit is the smallest unit independently assigned a treatment. Five leaves measured on each of four treated plants do not create twenty independently treated plants. A null hypothesis specifies a reference claim, such as zero difference in population means. A test statistic measures discrepancy from that claim relative to sampling variation. A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that a result will replicate. Choose the significance level and primary question before inspecting outcomes. sections.title: Worked example uncertainty in a mean
sections.body: For independent observations with unknown population variance, a two-sided confidence interval for a population mean is \bar\ \pm\ t_\frac}. The critical value comes from a Student t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. It is larger than the normal critical value when the sample is small, reflecting additional uncertainty in estimating the variance. The interval is approximately 4.03 to 5.27 t/ha. It estimates a population mean under the sampling assumptions; it is not an interval containing 95% of individual plot yields. Four conveniently selected plots would not justify population inference merely because the formula can be evaluated. For a two-sample comparison, the same principle estimates a difference and its standard error. Welch's method estimates variance contributions separately and adjusts the reference degrees of freedom. For a paired comparison, apply the one-sample idea to within-pair differences.

sections.title: One-sample and two-sample t-tests
sections.body: PlantGrowth is a real dataset supplied with R containing dry-weight measurements for a control and two treatment groups. The documentation does not identify the treatments as fertilizer rates, so do not invent that interpretation. The one-sample example asks whether the population mean control weight differs from 5 in the dataset's measurement units. The reference value is an illustrative benchmark, not a verified agronomic target. For two independent groups, Welch's t-test allows unequal population variances and is R's default. Define the contrast order explicitly so the sign of the estimate is unambiguous. The t-test assumes independent observations and appropriate conditions for inference on the mean. With small samples, inspect strong skewness and outliers; normality of model errors matters more than the appearance of a pooled distribution. Welch's test relaxes equal variance, not independence. Do not choose a one-sided alternative after seeing the sign of the difference.

sections.title: Paired observations
sections.body: A paired design compares linked observations, such as before-and-after measurements on the same plots. The analysis uses within-pair differences. It differs from treating the two measurements as unrelated groups. Pairs must be correctly matched; the differences should be independent across pairs. Normality is assessed for differences, not separately for before and after values. Without an untreated comparison, a before–after increase may reflect time or seasonal effects as well as management.

sections.title: Chi-square tests for pest observations
sections.body: A contingency table cross-classifies counts. In the simulated pest dataset, each independently treated plot contributes one yes/no infestation status at a specified assessment date. sections.title: Why ANOVA?
sections.body: Comparing three or more means by many unadjusted t-tests increases the chance of false-positive conclusions. One-way analysis of variance begins with a global null hypothesis that all group population means are equal. Its model is Y_=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_, where \tau_i represents a treatment effect and the errors are assumed independent with mean zero and common variance. Normal errors provide the classical small-sample F reference distribution. The test compares treatment mean square with residual mean square. A large F-statistic means between-group variation is large relative to unexplained within-group variation.

sections.title: Worked calculation separating sources of variation
sections.body: Suppose three independently randomized groups have yields A = (3, 4, 5), B = (4, 5, 6), and C = (5, 6, 7) t/ha. The group means are 4, 5, and 6 and the grand mean is 5. For equal group size 3, treatment sum of squares is 3[(4-5)^2+(5-5)^2+(6-5)^2]=6. Within each group the squared deviations add to 2, giving residual sum of squares 6 across all groups. There are 3 - 1 = 2 treatment degrees of freedom and 9 - 3 = 6 residual degrees of freedom. Treatment mean square is 6/2 = 3, residual mean square is 6/6 = 1, and the F-statistic is 3. The p-value is 0.125. The observed means differ, but the data do not reject the global equality hypothesis at the conventional 0.05 level under this model. “Means differ in this sample” and “there is strong evidence of population differences” are distinct statements. Larger, well-designed replication may improve precision; repeating measurements of the same experimental units does not create new independent replication.

Tukey's method adjusts simultaneous pairwise comparisons within the specified family. Each row reports a signed difference, interval, and adjusted p-value. Read the group order carefully. Avoid reducing the entire analysis to letter groupings; report means, differences, uncertainty, and design.

sections.body: Residual-versus-fitted plots reveal unequal spread and patterns; normal quantile plots reveal departures from a normal error distribution. Neither a diagnostic plot nor a formal normality test can establish independence; that comes from the design. Small samples provide little information about distribution tails. If variances differ substantially, Welch's one-way test is an alternative for independent groups Welch's test does not use the ordinary equal-variance ANOVA error term. Do not follow it automatically with classical TukeyHSD(); choose pairwise methods compatible with unequal variances if needed.

sections.body: A useful report identifies the design, factor levels, independent replication, model, and any exclusions before presenting the table. Report treatment estimates with units, the global test and relevant degrees of freedom, the method used for comparisons, and the main diagnostic findings. sections.title: Association is not a treatment effect
sections.body: Pearson's correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between quantitative variables. Spearman's correlation applies Pearson's idea to ranks and describes monotonic association. Neither establishes causation, and a value near zero need not imply the absence of a nonlinear relationship. Both can be distorted by pooling unlike groups or by dependence among observations. The simulated farm_yield.csv contains 100 independent teaching records with nitrogen application, seasonal rainfall, and yield. It is constructed for a regression lesson and is not evidence for a real fertilizer recommendation. Inspect scatter plots before interpreting a correlation coefficient. Pearson's usual test assumes independent pairs and a suitable bivariate sampling model; ranks do not fix clustering or confounding. Spearman's test uses an approximation here because rounded measurements can create ties.

sections.title: Simple linear regression
sections.body: The model Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\epsilon_i describes a conditional mean response. The intercept is the predicted mean when X=0; the slope is a change in mean response per unit increase in X. Least squares minimizes squared residuals. The regression direction matters a model predicting yield from nitrogen is not interchangeable with one predicting nitrogen from yield. The slope has units t/ha of yield per kg/ha of applied nitrogen. Its estimate is an association in these data, conditional on the specified model. If zero nitrogen lies outside the observed range, the intercept is an extrapolation and need not have a useful agronomic interpretation.

sections.title: Worked calculation what least squares estimates
sections.body: For a simple regression with an intercept, the estimated slope is b_1=\frac)(y_i-\bar)})^2},\qquad b_0=\bar-b_1\bar. The slope is undefined when every predictor value is identical the denominator is zero. A range of predictor values is necessary to estimate a relationship. The calculation below verifies the coefficients from lm() rather than treating its output as a black box. Residuals are observed minus fitted responses. With an intercept, least squares makes their sum approximately zero. This algebraic property does not show that their errors are independent or normally distributed. Those require design knowledge and diagnostics.

sections.title: Multiple regression and conditional coefficients
sections.body: The nitrogen coefficient now describes a change while rainfall is held fixed in the model. It may differ from the simple-regression coefficient because the models ask different questions. Omitted confounders, measurement error, and nonlinearity can still bias interpretation. Adding predictors raises ordinary R^2 even if they contribute little; high R^2 does not establish causality or reliable future prediction. Strongly correlated predictors make separate coefficients unstable. In the crop trial, treatment and applied nitrogen are closely linked, so including both without thought can make individual effects hard to interpret. Select predictors using scientific reasoning, design, and an evaluation plan rather than repeated p-value searches.

sections.title: Residuals, leverage, and influence
sections.body: The residual-versus-fitted plot checks mean structure, the Q–Q plot checks the error distribution, the scale-location plot checks spread, and leverage/influence diagnostics identify observations that can strongly affect estimates. Check influential records against source information; do not delete them merely to improve fit. Classical t-tests and intervals need assumptions about errors, including independence and constant variance. Normality concerns the errors for small-sample inference, not every predictor's marginal distribution.

sections.title: Categorical predictors and reference levels
sections.body: Regression can include categorical variables through indicator coding. A two-variety example illustrates this without requiring the varieties to be interpreted as numeric doses. The reference level determines the intercept's meaning, while the fitted mean for each observation remains unchanged under a consistent recoding. The varietyB coefficient compares B with A conditional on the other terms in this additive model. It assumes a common variety difference across treatments. The preceding ANOVA chapter explains how a treatment-by-variety interaction relaxes that assumption. ANOVA and regression are connected expressions of linear modelling, rather than unrelated procedures selected solely by the appearance of a response column.

sections.title: Residual standard error and explained variation
sections.body: The residual sum of squares measures unexplained squared deviations after fitting. Dividing by residual degrees of freedom and taking a square root gives the residual standard error, in yield units. R^2 compares residual sum of squares with the total sum of squares around the observed mean R^2=1-\frac_i)^2})^2}. An in-sample R^2 describes fit to the observed response variation under that model. It is not the percentage probability that a prediction is correct. A narrow predictor range can produce a low R^2 even when a small slope is estimated usefully; a common time trend can produce a high R^2 for an unsuitable causal interpretation. Compare models in relation to their purpose and predictor domain.

sections.title: Nonlinearity and an apparent fertilizer optimum
sections.body: Crop response to a nutrient may increase initially and then approach a plateau or decline. A straight line over a restricted range can approximate part of that response without defining a biological optimum. A quadratic model adds a squared predictor term. In R formulas, write I(x^2) so the power is interpreted arithmetically. For a concave quadratic a+bN+cN^2 with c<0, its mathematical maximum occurs at -b/(2c). If c is positive, the stationary point is a minimum, not an optimum. Even a concave fitted curve may place its maximum outside the observed nitrogen range, where it is unsupported extrapolation. The supplied simulation is generated with a linear mean response, so a quadratic term should not be presented as discovering a true fertilizer optimum. An economic optimum additionally depends on crop price, input cost, and an appropriate response function. A fitted yield curve alone cannot supply those missing quantities. sections.title: Predict and evaluate honestly
sections.body: A confidence interval concerns the mean response at the specified predictors; a prediction interval includes variation in a new observation and is wider. Both rely on the model. Avoid extrapolation outside the training range and consider combinations of predictors that may be unusual even when each is individually within range. A random holdout is suitable for these independent simulated records. For repeated farms, spatial clusters, or time series, split by group, location, or time as appropriate. Fit preprocessing steps using training data only. One split gives an unstable estimate, so cross-validation may be needed for serious model comparison. The test set should not become another training set through repeated tuning.

chapters.title: Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
chapters.objectives: Combine explanation with executable analysis, distinguish .Rmd from .qmd, add tables and figures, render HTML/PDF/Word reports, and share a project that runs in a fresh session.

sections.title: A report is an argument supported by evidence
sections.body: A useful report states a question, describes data and design, explains decisions, presents results, and discusses limitations. Embedding R code keeps numerical evidence connected to its computation. If a dataset changes, re-rendering updates the results. This reduces transcription errors but cannot correct an unsuitable analysis. R Markdown usually uses .Rmd source files and rmarkdownrender(). Quarto uses .qmd source files and the quarto render command. Both can execute R through knitr. Their configuration differs R Markdown uses output whereas Quarto uses format. Simply renaming an old bookdown file is not a complete migration; chapter configuration, references, chunk options, and dependencies need checking.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Quarto document
sections.body: The following is a complete small document. The YAML header defines metadata and formats, ordinary Markdown supplies prose, and the R chunk computes a table. Save it as report.qmd in the project folder. The separate practicals/report.qmd provides a fuller working example. | label tbl-weight | tbl-cap "Mean dry weight by group in PlantGrowth." data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets") tab <- aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, mean) knitrkable(tab, digits = 2) Use descriptive chunk labels; figure labels begin with fig- and table labels with tbl- for cross-references. A figure chunk can use | fig-cap "...". A hidden setup chunk may set | include false, but keep the source available to readers. echo false hides code, not results. eval false displays an example without executing it. Avoid hiding warnings until they have been investigated.

sections.title: Dynamic values, figures, and interactive output
sections.body: Inline R inserts a computed value into a sentence. For example, write the literal source r nrow(PlantGrowth) to report the number of observations. This keeps prose synchronized with the data. Do not hard-code a p-value in the discussion while the model updates elsewhere. Use knitrkable() for simple portable tables and ordinary R plots for graphics. HTML widgets such as Plotly need an HTML output context. In multi-format documents, test knitris_html_output() and use a static plot for PDF and Word, as demonstrated in the visualization chapter.

sections.title: R Markdown remains part of the syllabus
sections.body: The supplied practicals/report.Rmd demonstrates the same analysis in R Markdown. Its header lists html_document, pdf_document, and word_document. Run these commands in the R Console from the project root

sections.title: Render and share
sections.body: Run shell commands in the Terminal, not in the R Console PDF output requires a working LaTeX distribution, for example TinyTeX installed through quarto install tinytex. Install it only if PDF is needed. HTML is the default classroom format in the README instructions. Rendering the entire book to Word or PDF combines chapters into a single document. Opening an HTML file locally is not the same as publishing it to a public server. Before sharing, restart R and render from source. Include source files, permitted data, metadata, package requirements, and instructions. sessionInfo() records R and loaded package versions. For a stable course release, consider a reviewed renv lockfile; do not claim that a package list alone pins an environment.

sections.title: Building the report in stages
sections.body: Let us develop a report in the same order as an analysis. First create the document with its question, data source, and design, even before the final model is chosen. Then add a data-check section, followed by descriptive tables and figures. Only after examining those results should the methods and model sections be completed. This sequence makes the scientific argument visible rather than hiding it behind a final table of p-values. An effective data section identifies the observational unit, sample size, variable units, collection period, and treatment or sampling scheme. State how the raw file was obtained and whether permission is needed to share it. In the cleaning section, explain missingness, corrections, and exclusions with their consequences for the analysis. Avoid including personal or confidential identifiers merely because they happen to be in the original spreadsheet. The methods section should name the response, predictors or factors, model, and assumptions in terms that m

sections.title: Managing code chunks and dependencies
sections.body: Each document is easiest to understand when it can be executed from top to bottom in a new session. The first chunk loads packages and reads inputs. Later chunks depend on those named objects. Avoid loading data by hand into the Environment pane and then assuming they will be available during rendering. | label setup | include false library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) trial <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv") stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(trialplot_id)) | label tbl-treatment-means | tbl-cap "Mean simulated grain yield by management treatment." means <- trial |> group_by(treatment) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop") knitrkable(means, digits = 2) The setup chunk is hidden in the displayed report but remains in the source. It does not install packages. The table chunk visibly records the summary operation. A future reader can distinguish a count of plot records from an estimate of mean yield and can rerun both. Caching and freezing can save time in large projects

sections.title: Tables, figures, and numerical precision
sections.body: A table title should say what was measured, how observations were grouped, and what the numbers represent. Put units in column headings where possible. Report enough digits for interpretation without suggesting unrealistic measurement precision. A yield measured to 0.01 t/ha should not normally be presented to eight decimal places merely because R printed them. A figure caption should allow the graph to be understood away from the surrounding paragraph. Distinguish observed points from fitted lines, and describe error bars or shaded intervals precisely. “Error bars” is insufficient are they SD, SE, confidence intervals, or prediction intervals? If an interactive figure permits hovering, retain axis labels and a caption so the static version remains meaningful. Cross-references are preferable to manually typed numbers. After inserting a new table, @tbl-treatment-means updates its reference automatically. Manually writing “Table 3” can become wrong after reorganization. The same applies

sections.title: Reproducibility is also a classroom assessment
sections.body: Ask a classmate to open a copy of the complete project, restart R, and render the report. If it fails, identify whether the missing component is a file, package, path, or undocumented manual step. Record the correction in the project instead of asking the classmate to imitate your Console history. Finally, read the rendered document as a reader. Are headings in a logical order? Do tables fit? Are captions readable? Do the conclusions match the estimates? A report can be computationally reproducible and scientifically weak, or scientifically thoughtful but computationally incomplete. Undergraduate training should develop both skills together.

sections.title: Vibe coding and AI-assisted R programming
sections.body: From an idea to a first draft Vibe coding is an informal term for developing software by describing what you want in ordinary language, asking an AI system to generate code, running it, and requesting changes. The term is often associated with accepting implementation details without examining them closely. For a statistical analysis, we need to go further understand the code, verify the calculations, and justify the model. In this book, we use the conversational approach as an entry into reviewed AI-assisted programming. See the overview of the term. For example, a student might begin with “Make a colourful graph of crop yields.” An AI assistant can draft a plot quickly, but that request omits the data structure, units, experimental unit, and purpose.
